items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Among them was Sarah Vaughan... while Sarah Vaughan was singing, there was something I played behind her, which must have impressed her. She turned around and looked at me and smiled.

ctx.x: Anyway. the Collegians -- now there was a black college dance-band community. The Pittsburgh Courier, the black weekly newspaper, established a Negro college dance-band poll in 1947. The winner of this poll got a trip to New York, a performance at Carnegie Hall on an all-star program, and a performance at the Savoy

Ballroom, the track. This program at Carnegie Hall was one of those gala all stars. Actually the winners of the Pittsburgh Courier music poll -- I don’t know if they called it the jazz poll. It probably was a jazz poll -- but such stars as Lucky Millinder, Bill Eckstine, Count Basie, Sarah Vaughan, Duke Ellington.

items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: like Sarah Vaughan, usually let me have free hand

ctx.x: Can you tell us about writing for Joe Williams? You wrote a certain style for him, and what it was like to work with him when he was with the band?

It was great working with him because he, like Sarah Vaughan, usually let me have free hand, free reign, and just let me have the lyrics and he’d sing them down for me, and give me an idea of basically the kind of backing he wanted, and let me go myself from there. ‘Cause I used to pride myself on being able to really write some Basie type blues.

items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: Quincy Jones commissioned me to do an album with Sarah Vaughan and there was a varied type of instrumental group there.

ctx.x: Eleven years, wow. And you had mentioned Sinatra, and thinking about vocalists, did the guys in the band ever kind of resent the vocalist being out front and doing four or five songs a night and was that something that you guys felt like you didn’t feel it was necessary?

Well the professionalism in this particular orchestra didn’t allow for that kind of attitude on a large scale. And we loved Sinatra, we loved Billy Eckstine, we loved Sarah Vaughan and we loved Tony Bennett, and there just was no feeling of that kind. Whenever we knew we were going to work with them we said well we’re going to have some fun now. Some others, who shall remain nameless, we didn’t have as much fun with because some of them didn’t have the quality arrangements that we would like to play, and some of…
Well you certainly had a powerhouse band there for those years, plus with Joe Williams on board, and a great time. Fortunately you recorded a lot so it’s documented. © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-
